blocks.text: 1.1.3 Type Casting and Conversion

Type casting and conversion are fundamental concepts in Java that allow changing a value from one data type to another. This process is crucial for manipulating data and ensuring type safety in various programming scenarios.
Key Concepts:

items: Implicit Casting (Widening):
Automatic conversion of a smaller data type to a larger data type.
The magnitude is never lost, but int or long to float, and long to double, can lose precision: `float f = 123456789;` stores 1.23456792E8.
Example: int to long, float to double.
Explicit Casting (Narrowing):
Manual conversion of a larger data type to a smaller data type.
Potential data loss can occur.
Requires explicit syntax: (targetType) value.
Example: double to int, long to int.
Primitive to Object Conversion (Boxing):
Converting a primitive type to its corresponding wrapper class.
Example: int to Integer, char to Character.
Object to Primitive Conversion (Unboxing):
Converting a wrapper class object to its corresponding primitive type.
Example: Integer to int, Character to char.
String Conversions:
Converting primitives or objects to Strings.
Converting Strings to primitives or objects.

blocks.text: Best Practices:
Remember, premature optimization is the root of all evil. Only optimize after profiling and identifying real bottlenecks.

items: Always check for potential data loss when performing narrowing conversions.
Use wrapper class methods for safe conversions (e.g., Integer.parseInt()).
Handle potential exceptions when converting Strings to numbers.
Be aware of auto-boxing and unboxing performance implications in loops.

blocks.text: Java 21 Features:
While type casting fundamentals remain unchanged, Java 21 continues to improve type inference and pattern matching, which can sometimes reduce the need for explicit casting.
Common Pitfalls:

items: Loss of precision in floating-point to integer conversions.
Integer overflow when casting between integer types.
Runtime exceptions when casting incompatible reference types.

blocks.text: Interview Insights:

items: Q: Explain the difference between implicit and explicit casting in Java. When would you use each?
A: Implicit casting, also known as widening conversion, occurs automatically when converting a smaller data type to a larger one. For example:

blocks.text:
int myInt = 100;
long myLong = myInt; // Implicit casting from int to long

This is safe because every int value fits exactly in a long (int to float would not be: it can round). Explicit casting, or narrowing conversion, is used when converting a larger data type to a smaller one. It requires manual intervention:

double myDouble = 3.14;
int myInt = (int) myDouble; // Explicit casting from double to int

Explicit casting is necessary when there's a risk of data loss. In this case, the fractional part of the double is truncated. Best practice: Always use explicit casting when there's a potential for data loss, and be aware of the consequences.

items: Q: What are the risks associated with narrowing conversions, and how can you mitigate them?
A: The main risks of narrowing conversions are:
Loss of precision: When converting from floating-point to integer types.
Overflow: When the value exceeds the range of the target type. Example of precision loss:

blocks.text:
double price = 19.99;
int roundedPrice = (int) price; // roundedPrice will be 19
Example of overflow:

long bigNumber = 2147483648L; // Exceeds Integer.MAX_VALUE
int convertedNumber = (int) bigNumber; // Results in -2147483648 due to overflow

b. Use proper rounding for floating-point to integer conversions:

double price = 19.99;
int roundedPrice = (int) Math.round(price); // roundedPrice will be 20
